findings.title: Cleartext HTTP OSS model/checkpoint downloads are loaded with unsafe torch.load (pickle RCE).
findings.description: SPACE-1 and SPACE-3 READMEs instruct users to download pretrained models and fine-tuned checkpoints over plaintext HTTP from Alibaba OSS host datarepo0.oss-cn-hangzhou-zmf.aliyuncs.com (model.zip / outputs.zip and related archives). After unzip, training and inference scripts pass those paths as --init_checkpoint. The trainers call torch.load on '{init_checkpoint}.model' with no weights_only / integrity check, which deserializes a pickle-based PyTorch object graph. SPACE-2 documents the same HTTP OSS URLs but ships only a README in this tree. SPACE-3 Trippy additionally loads HTTP-sourced Hugging Face-format directories via from_pretrained (historically torch.load of pytorch_model.bin).
findings.impact: A network attacker who can MITM the HTTP download (or who compromises the public OSS object) can replace the zip with a malicious checkpoint. When the victim runs the documented infer/train scripts, torch.load executes attacker-controlled Python on the training/inference host (userland RCE, credential and GPU/data access).
findings.attack_path:
1. Victim follows space-1/README.md (or space-3/README.md) and downloads model.zip or outputs.zip from http://datarepo0.oss-cn-hangzhou-zmf.aliyuncs.com/... over HTTP, then unzips into model/ or ${SAVE_ROOT}/outputs as instructed.
2. On-path attacker (or bucket object tampering) supplies a zip whose checkpoint file is a malicious torch serialization gadget rather than real weights.
3. Victim runs scripts such as space-1/scripts/multiwoz2.1/infer.sh, which sets INIT_CHECKPOINT to the downloaded checkpoint path and invokes run.py --init_checkpoint=...
4. space-1/galaxy/trainers/trainer.py load() (and pretrain_trainer.py; space-3/space/trainers/trainer.py and gen_trainer.py) execute torch.load(f'{init_checkpoint}.model', ...) with default pickle deserialization, achieving code execution as the user running the script.
findings.remediation: Serve all model and checkpoint URLs exclusively over HTTPS with certificate validation. Publish checksums (SHA-256) in the README and verify before unzip. Prefer torch.load(..., weights_only=True) on modern PyTorch, or load state dicts from safetensors. Treat OSS objects as untrusted input until verified.
findings.poc_video_notes: No live exploit video: delivering a torch pickle gadget against a victim host is out of scope. The HTTP URLs, unzip instructions, init_checkpoint wiring, and torch.load call sites are confirmed in-tree. From this environment the zmf OSS endpoint timed out (internal-range DNS); the public hangzhou endpoint redirects clients to that zmf endpoint, and the READMEs still prescribe plaintext http:// URLs.

findings.title: Cleartext HTTP wget of training zip unzipped into the git root allows MITM code overwrite.
findings.description: sdsql/README.md tells users to wget http://binhua-poc.oss-cn-beijing.aliyuncs.com/sqlova_data.zip into the repository root and run unzip with no destination jail, member allowlist, or checksum. The archive is expected to supply training JSON consumed later by the sqlova pipeline. There is no ZipFile path sanitization layer in-repo; extraction relies on system unzip. Lab confirmation: Info-ZIP strips ../ and absolute prefixes, but happily overwrites same-directory members such as sdsql/train.py when those paths appear in the zip. The documented host still speaks HTTP; the named bucket currently returns NoSuchBucket, which does not remove the MITM overwrite chain when a user runs the published commands.
findings.impact: An on-path attacker can return a forged zip that overwrites project Python (for example sdsql/train.py or sqlova utilities). The next python train.py / infer invocation executes attacker code as the developer user. Secondary impact is integrity loss of competition data and submission artifacts.
findings.attack_path:
1. Victim follows sdsql/README.md and runs wget over HTTP for sqlova_data.zip, then unzip sqlova_data.zip at the git root.
2. Attacker MITMs the cleartext response (bucket need not exist) and returns HTTP 200 with a zip whose members include sdsql/train.py or other importable project paths containing malicious code.
3. System unzip extracts into the cwd and overwrites those files (confirmed with UnZip 6.00: member sdsql/train.py replaces the real file; ../ traversal is stripped but in-tree overwrite succeeds).
4. Victim runs python train.py as documented; the overwritten module executes attacker code. Separately, trained checkpoints are later loaded via torch.load in sdsql/train.py:180-189 if the attacker also plants model bins under output_dir.
findings.remediation: Switch the download URL to HTTPS, pin a SHA-256 of the archive, and extract into an empty data directory with a safe extractor that rejects unexpected member paths (especially any path under sdsql/ or .github/). Do not unzip archives into the repository root.
findings.poc_video_notes: Overwrite behavior was reproduced locally with a crafted zip and unzip -o (member sdsql/train.py replaced). Full MITM against a live user was not recorded. Anonymous GET to binhua-poc.oss-cn-beijing.aliyuncs.com currently returns NoSuchBucket; the README still publishes the cleartext wget command.

findings.title: Hardcoded default MySQL username/password used for ATIS execution checks.
findings.description: R2SQL ships CLI defaults --database_username and --database_password both set to the same fixed string (variable names database_username / database_password in parse_args for sparc and cosql). sql_util.execution_results connects via pymysql.connect(user=..., password=...) with no host argument (localhost), then runs cursor.execute("use atis3;") before executing model-predicted SQL. Function signatures in model_util default database_password to an empty string, but the interactive/metrics path asserts a non-empty password before use, so the empty-string default is not a live auth bypass. There is no networked demo server in this tree; impact requires an operator who creates a MySQL account matching those defaults (or leaves a local ATIS install with them) and enables execution metrics.
findings.impact: Anyone with local (or mis-bound) MySQL access using the documented default credentials can run arbitrary SQL in the atis3 schema through the evaluation helpers, including destructive statements if the MySQL account is privileged. This is a credential-hygiene / local eval footgun rather than a remote unauthenticated service bug.
findings.attack_path:
1. Operator installs MySQL for ATIS-style execution accuracy and (explicitly or by copying common EditSQL/ATIS setups) creates a user matching the argparse defaults database_username / database_password.
2. Operator runs r2sql evaluation with compute_metrics / executable checks so run.py passes those defaults into model_util and sql_util.execution_results.
3. pymysql.connect authenticates to localhost with the hardcoded defaults; the session switches to database atis3.
4. Model predictions (or a locally modified prediction file) are executed as SQL in that session. If MySQL is also exposed beyond localhost with the same account, a remote attacker with network reach can reuse the published default password; the code itself does not bind a remote listener.
findings.remediation: Remove hardcoded credential defaults; require environment variables or a local secrets file that is gitignored. Keep MySQL bound to localhost with a unique strong password. Prefer the sqlite evaluation path already used elsewhere in r2sql when possible.
findings.poc_video_notes: No video: no MySQL/ATIS instance is running in the scan environment. Defaults, localhost connect, use atis3, and the non-empty password assert are confirmed in source. Empty database_password defaults are not a working bypass.
